units.title: Introduction to Automata Theory
topics: Finite automata as language acceptor and translator
Conversion between Mealy and Moore machines

important_questions.question: Define finite automaton.
important_questions.answer: A finite automaton is a mathematical machine with a finite number of states. It reads an input string one symbol at a time and changes state according to its transition function. It accepts a string if it finishes in a final state.

important_questions.question: Differentiate Moore machine and Mealy machine.
important_questions.answer: A Moore machine produces output based only on its present state, whereas a Mealy machine produces output based on its present state and current input. Moore outputs are written on states; Mealy outputs are written on transitions. Mealy machines often need fewer states, while Moore outputs are generally more stable.

important_questions.question: Explain the structure of a finite automaton with a neat diagram.
important_questions.answer: A finite automaton consists of a finite set of states (Q), input alphabet (Σ), transition function (δ), start state (q0), and final states (F). It processes each input symbol and moves to the next state. Acceptance occurs when the input is completely read and the current state belongs to F.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart LR
A([Start]) --> B[Read input symbol]
B --> C{Transition function δ}
C --> D[Next state]
D -->|More input| B
D -->|Input finished| E{Final state?}
E -->|Yes| F([Accept])
E -->|No| G([Reject])

important_questions.question: What is the difference between DFA and NFA?
important_questions.answer: In a DFA, for each state and input symbol exactly one next state exists. In an NFA, zero, one or many next states may be possible. Both recognize regular languages.

important_questions.question: What is a regular expression? Give examples.
important_questions.answer: A regular expression is an algebraic notation used to describe a regular language. For alphabet {0,1}, (0+1)* represents all binary strings, including the empty string; 0(0+1)* represents strings beginning with 0.

important_questions.question: Explain the subset construction method for converting NFA into DFA.
important_questions.answer: Start with the set containing the NFA start state (or its epsilon-closure). Treat every set of NFA states as one DFA state. For each input symbol, collect all reachable NFA states and take epsilon-closure if needed. Repeat until no new sets are generated. Any set containing an NFA final state becomes a DFA final state.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
A([NFA start state]) --> B[Create initial state-set]
B --> C[For each input symbol, find reachable states]
C --> D[Create a new state-set]
D --> E{Any unseen state-set?}
E -->|Yes| C
E -->|No| F[Mark sets containing NFA final state]
F --> G([Equivalent DFA])

important_questions.question: What is a context-free grammar (CFG)?
important_questions.answer: A CFG is a four-tuple G=(V,Σ,P,S), where V is the set of variables, Σ is the set of terminals, P is the set of production rules and S is the start symbol. Each production has one variable on its left side.

important_questions.question: Explain ambiguity in grammar.
important_questions.answer: A grammar is ambiguous if at least one string generated by it has more than one distinct parse tree or more than one leftmost/rightmost derivation. Ambiguity can create multiple interpretations of the same expression.

important_questions.question: Explain Chomsky hierarchy of grammars.
important_questions.answer: The Chomsky hierarchy classifies grammars into four levels: Type-0 unrestricted, Type-1 context-sensitive, Type-2 context-free and Type-3 regular. Their language classes are progressively more restricted: regular is a subset of context-free, which is a subset of context-sensitive, which is a subset of recursively enumerable languages.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TB
A[Type 0: Unrestricted] --> B[Type 1: Context-sensitive]
B --> C[Type 2: Context-free]
C --> D[Type 3: Regular]

important_questions.question: What is a Pushdown Automaton?
important_questions.answer: A Pushdown Automaton (PDA) is a finite automaton equipped with a stack. The stack gives it additional memory and enables it to recognize context-free languages.

important_questions.question: Differentiate finite automaton and pushdown automaton.
important_questions.answer: A finite automaton has only finite-state memory and recognizes regular languages. A PDA has an additional stack, can store an unbounded stack sequence, and recognizes context-free languages. Example: a PDA can recognize balanced parentheses.

important_questions.question: Explain the working of a Pushdown Automaton with diagram.
important_questions.answer: A PDA reads an input symbol, checks the top of its stack, changes state and may push or pop stack symbols. Acceptance can be by final state or empty stack, depending on the definition. The stack helps match nested structures such as balanced parentheses.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart LR
A([Input string]) --> B[Finite control]
B <--> C[(Stack memory)]
B --> D{Input consumed and acceptance condition met?}
D -->|Yes| E([Accept])
D -->|No| F([Reject])

units.title: Turing Machine
topics: Multi-tape, multi-head and multidimensional Turing machines

important_questions.question: Define Turing Machine.
important_questions.answer: A Turing Machine is an abstract model of computation consisting of a finite control, an infinite tape and a read/write head. It reads and writes symbols and moves its head left or right according to transition rules.

important_questions.question: Differentiate decidable and undecidable problems.
important_questions.answer: A decidable problem has an algorithm/Turing machine that halts on every input and gives the correct yes/no answer. An undecidable problem has no algorithm that correctly decides every possible input and always halts.

important_questions.question: Explain the Halting Problem and why it is undecidable.
important_questions.answer: The Halting Problem asks whether a given program or Turing Machine eventually stops on a particular input. It is undecidable: assuming a universal algorithm could always answer this question leads to a self-contradiction by constructing a program that does the opposite of the prediction about itself.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
A([Program + input]) --> B[Hypothetical halting decider]
B --> C{Will it halt?}
C -->|Yes| D[Construct loop forever]
C -->|No| E[Construct halt immediately]
D --> F[Contradiction]
E --> F
